# ISLA, one idea at a time {#sec-isla}

**ISLA is a slice-attention transformer that never sees a coordinate.**
Every learned operation inside it acts on scalars that do not change when
the geometry is rotated, translated or uniformly rescaled. Every sum it
takes over the boundary is a quadrature rule, so its answer converges to one
field as the mesh is refined instead of depending on where the mesher put
its cells. Vectors are rebuilt at the very end from a basis that rotates
with the body. That is the whole design. The rest of this chapter builds it
up in six ideas, each with a picture on the two-dimensional airfoil of
@sec-problem, and then states the result as the tests that verify it. What
the design buys and costs in measured error is the business of the evidence
chapters. This one carries no standings.

The chapter reads top to bottom with every collapsed note closed. The notes
hold derivations and code correspondences for a reader who wants them.

```{python}
#| label: setup-isla
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize
```

## Where ISLA stands among slice-attention transformers {#sec-isla-position}

**ISLA keeps the slice-attention mechanism of the Transolver family and
changes only what the network is allowed to see.** That family holds the
strongest empirical record on industrial aerodynamics. Its *physics
attention* routes every mesh point softly into a few hundred *slices*, lets
the slices attend to one another, and reads the result back to the points.
GeoTransolver adds a geometry encoder and a global-context projector. Both
feed the network raw coordinates in some frame and the problem's global
vector as a raw feature. Both learn the physics of pose and scale from data,
and both aggregate over whatever points the mesher produced.

The change is paid once at the network's edges: invariant scalars on the way
in, an equivariant basis on the way out. Inside, the slice layers are the
same kind of object as Transolver's, with two additions that this chapter
explains: the routing weights carry the surface measure, and every token
knows where it is only relative to the slice anchors (routing, anchors and
read-back are defined in ideas 3 and 5). The opposite design enforces
physical structure inside every layer, with typed scalar and vector streams
or analytic boundary-integral kernels; what that costs on separated
three-dimensional flow is @sec-interior-negatives. The whole pass, stage by
stage with every tensor shape, is drawn once in @fig-isla-pass. Each of the
six ideas below maps onto one of its stages.

## What goes in and what comes out {#sec-isla-inputs}

**ISLA maps a sampled boundary plus the problem's global conditions to
fields at query points.** Per case, the inputs are:

- $N$ sampled boundary points $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, each with a unit
  outward normal $n_i$ (a hat, $\hat n_i$, marks a unit vector below, and
  the model renormalizes the normals it is given) and a **measure weight**
  $w_i > 0$, the surface area the point stands for, so that
  $\sum_i w_i f(x_i) \approx \int f\,dA$. Under the reporting protocol of
  @sec-protocol, $N = 200{,}000$ per case.
- **Global vector inputs** $g_k \in \mathbb{R}^3$, $k = 1,\dots,K$:
  directions that belong to the problem rather than to any cell. External
  aerodynamics, the benchmark instance of this book, has $K = 1$, and $g_1$
  is the far-field flow direction. A buoyant flow passes gravity, and a
  magnetized flow adds the applied field. Steady conduction with pinned
  temperatures has $K = 0$. The model normalizes each to a unit direction
  $\hat g_k$. A magnitude that matters is a global scalar.
- **Global scalar inputs** $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^S$: the parameters of the
  PDE, such as a diffusivity, a Reynolds number or a far-field speed. They
  are appended to the seed of every token. The surface tasks of this book
  have $S = 0$. The AirfRANS interior task has $S = 1$, the inlet speed.
- Optionally, per-cell boundary data (declared in `boundary_schema`) and
  per-query fields (declared in `query_schema`). The boundary data is whatever a boundary
  condition prescribes at each cell, as named fields of declared tensor
  rank: a condition tag or a Dirichlet trace at rank 0, a prescribed
  traction at rank 1, a prescribed stress at rank 2. A per-query field is a
  material label or a source term at an interior query, at rank 0 or above.
  A field of rank 1 or 2 enters only through its invariants against the
  token's own directions (@sec-isla-inputs-rank).
- For prediction off the surface, the interior query positions $x_q$ and
  the boundary surface at full resolution (`boundary_geometry`; the tokens
  are a sample of it). The direction and the signed distance an interior
  token needs are functions of that surface and the query position, so the
  model computes them itself from the exact closest point of the surface
  (@sec-arch-modes), the same for every way the tokens were sampled. No
  stored signed-distance field is read.

The outputs are named fields of declared rank at the query points: scalar
fields (surface pressure, in every surface result of the book), vector
fields (wall shear stress), and tensors of rank 2 to 4 where a problem asks
for them (a stress tensor). On a surface task the queries *are* the surface
sample, and each point receives its own prediction. On the interior task,
query points off the surface join the sample as tokens
(@sec-interior-query-tokens). Names can nest. A field name can contain a
dot (`surface.pressure`), and the output is then a nested TensorDict, the
project's convention for a tree of fields. Every value of the declaration
is a leaf, so a dot is the only way to say "group", and there is no
ambiguity between a group and a rank spec.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-inputs
#| fig-cap: >
#|   What one token carries, on the running airfoil example. Each boundary
#|   cell (black dot at its midpoint) has a position, a unit outward normal
#|   (gray arrow) and a measure weight (the cell's length here, its area in
#|   three dimensions; drawn as the thickness of the boundary segment). The
#|   one global vector input of the example is the far-field flow direction
#|   (black arrow). How to read this: nothing else enters the model; in
#|   particular no coordinate of any point is ever given to a learned layer.
#| code-fold: true
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
# an uneven "mesher": fine near the leading edge, coarse elsewhere
u = np.linspace(0, 1, 2001)
density = 1.0 + 14.0 * np.exp(-((u - 0.5) / 0.05) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-((u - 0.0) / 0.04) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-((u - 1.0) / 0.04) ** 2)
cdf = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(density[:-1] * np.diff(u))]); cdf /= cdf[-1]
frac = np.interp(np.linspace(0, 1, 41), cdf, u)
Jm = joukowski(n_cells=40, frac=frac)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.6))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.5)
segs = np.stack([Jm["xy"][:-1], Jm["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[BASELINE], linewidths=2 + 14 * Jm["w"] / Jm["w"].max(), capstyle="butt", zorder=1))
ax.plot(Jm["xy"][:, 0], Jm["xy"][:, 1], color=INK, lw=0.8, zorder=2)
ax.quiver(Jm["mid"][:, 0], Jm["mid"][:, 1], Jm["nrm"][:, 0], Jm["nrm"][:, 1], color=MUTED, scale=12, width=0.0035, headwidth=4, zorder=3)
ax.plot(Jm["mid"][:, 0], Jm["mid"][:, 1], "o", ms=3.2, color=INK, zorder=4)
i = 8
ax.annotate(r"token $i$: position $x_i$, normal $n_i$, measure $w_i$", xy=Jm["mid"][i], xytext=(0.2, -1.15),
            fontsize=9.5, color=INK, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.8))
g = Jm["g_hat"]
ax.annotate("", xy=(-1.9 + 0.8 * g[0], 1.05 + 0.8 * g[1]), xytext=(-1.9, 1.05), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.0))
ax.text(-2.4, 1.3, r"global vector input $\hat g_1$ (far-field flow direction)", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
ax.text(1.05, 0.95, "thick segment = large measure weight\n(a coarse cell); thin = fine cell", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Tensor shapes and keyword names"}
Every constructor argument and every `forward` input is keyword-only.
Every field other than the geometry is *named* and carries a declared
tensor rank. The constructor takes `output_schema`, `global_schema`,
`boundary_schema` and `query_schema`. Each is a mapping from a field name
to a rank spec, the grammar every mesh model shares
(`physicsnemo.mesh.fields.FieldSchema.parse`): a mapping `{rank, symmetric,
parity}` whose `rank` is 0 for a scalar, 1 for a vector, 2 for a rank-2
tensor, and so on (a bare integer is not accepted; a mapping of mappings
is a nested group of fields). `symmetric` marks a fully symmetric
tensor and `parity: odd` marks a pseudotensor output. One name declares one field; several independent
scalars, such as a standardized parameter vector, are several rank-0 names.
`forward` takes the boundary as `boundary_meshes`, a mapping from a name to
a `Mesh` of codimension one whose cells are the tokens (centroid, normal
and effective measure), with the `boundary_schema` fields in each
mesh's `cell_data`; the per-case `global_schema` fields in `global_data`, a rank-1 field
a `(3,)` vector and a rank-0 field a scalar; and, on the interior task,
`prediction_points`, a point cloud carrying the `query_schema` fields in its
`point_data`. It returns a point-cloud `Mesh` with the outputs in its
`point_data`, `(N,)`, `(N, 3)` or `(N, 3, 3)` by rank. A prediction point's
direction and signed wall distance are computed inside the model from the
boundary surface (`boundary_geometry`, the same named boundaries at full
resolution; without it the tokens' own cells, when they are the whole
boundary); a dataset's stored signed-distance field enters, if
wanted, as a declared query input like any other datum (@sec-arch-modes).
Each named mapping can be given flat with dotted names, nested, or as a
TensorDict. The output is a TensorDict of batch size (batch, tokens) whose
leaves are the output names. A dotted name is unflattened into a group
(`out["surface", "pressure"]`). Each leaf has shape (batch, tokens, 3, ...,
3), with as many trailing axes as its rank. The $K$ rank-1 global inputs
are the global directions. The limits of the fused geometry kernel are
stated once, in @sec-isla-inputs-rank. The class is
`physicsnemo.experimental.models.ISLA`.
:::

## Idea 1: every sum over the boundary is a quadrature rule {#sec-isla-quadrature}

**A mesh is a discretization of a surface, not the surface itself, so any
quantity the model forms by summing over cells must be an integral estimate
that does not care how the cells were laid down.** A plain mean over points
depends on the mesher: refine the leading edge and the mean of anything is
pulled toward the leading edge. A *measure-weighted* mean,
$\sum_i w_i f_i / \sum_i w_i$, is a quadrature estimate of
$\int f\,dA / \int dA$ and converges to the same number under any
refinement. @fig-isla-quadrature shows the difference on the airfoil: two
"meshers" produce two samples of the same shape, and the plain means
disagree while the measure-weighted means agree.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-quadrature
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Two samplings of one airfoil, and the mean pressure coefficient each
#|   gives. Left: equal-arclength cells. Right: the same shape with cells
#|   clustered at the leading edge, as a mesher resolving the suction peak
#|   would. Color is the surface pressure coefficient. The plain mean over
#|   points (gray) moves between the two samplings because the second
#|   sampling has more points where the pressure is low; the measure-weighted
#|   mean (blue) is a quadrature estimate of the same integral and moves
#|   only by the quadrature error. How to read this: the slice sums inside
#|   ISLA are all of the blue kind. It does not show a trained model.
#| code-fold: true
Ju = joukowski(n_cells=40)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 3.9))
norm = Normalize(-1.6, 1.0)
for ax, JJ, title in zip(axes, (Ju, Jm), ("equal-arclength sampling", "leading-edge-clustered sampling")):
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.35, 1.3)
    segs = np.stack([JJ["xy"][:-1], JJ["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=DIVERGING(norm(np.clip(JJ["cp_s"], -1.6, 1))), linewidths=6, capstyle="butt", zorder=2))
    ax.plot(JJ["mid"][:, 0], JJ["mid"][:, 1], "o", ms=2.6, color=INK, zorder=3)
    plain = JJ["cp_s"].mean(); weighted = np.sum(JJ["w"] * JJ["cp_s"]) / JJ["w"].sum()
    ax.set_title(f"{title}: {len(JJ['w'])} cells")
    ax.text(0.0, -1.0, f"plain mean of $C_p$ over points: {plain:+.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
    ax.text(0.0, -1.22, f"measure-weighted mean: {weighted:+.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=BLUE, fontweight="bold")
sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=norm, cmap=DIVERGING); sm.set_array([])
cb = fig.colorbar(sm, ax=axes, fraction=0.025, pad=0.02); cb.set_label("surface pressure coefficient $C_p$ [–]", color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

In ISLA the measure enters through the routing softmax as a log-space bias,
$\ell_i \equiv \log w_i$. The weight a slice gives to a point is then
proportional to $w_i$ times a learned, content-dependent factor, so every
slice aggregate is a weighted mean of the blue kind. Under sampling laws
that do not draw cells uniformly, the recipe supplies the Horvitz–Thompson
weight (area divided by inclusion probability), and the estimate remains
consistent. The four draws the book uses are drawn side by side in
@fig-sampling-laws. This is the mechanism behind ISLA's consistency under a
change of sampling at inference and under a change of the sampling law it
is trained under. The evidence for both is in @sec-discretization-centerpiece
and @sec-robustness-density. The measure is a correctness requirement
rather than a tunable. Without the weights a slice aggregates a mean over
whichever points the mesher placed, and a different mesher changes the
answer (@sec-principle). Its in-distribution price is an estimator variance
that shrinks with the cell count and is gone at the reporting protocol
(@sec-equal-budget).

## Idea 2: position without a frame {#sec-isla-frame}

**A model that is handed coordinates in some frame must learn that the
frame is arbitrary. ISLA is never handed coordinates.** Two things are
needed to make this work: a unit of length, and a way to say where a point
is.

The unit of length is how far apart the boundary's points typically are.
Take every pair of sampled points, weight each pair by the measure the two
points stand for, and average their squared separation. The square root of
that average is $L$. It is a property of the boundary, not of the mesher,
because the weights are areas. It needs no center, because only differences
between points enter. It does not change when every weight is multiplied by
the same constant, because the weights are normalized to one before they
are used. And it stays finite under refinement on any boundary whose points
have a finite second moment. That includes fractal boundaries where the
total area itself keeps growing (the Koch-curve row of
@sec-isla-contracts). In symbols, with
$\tilde w_i \equiv w_i / \sum_j w_j$,

$$
L^2 \equiv \sum_{i,j} \tilde w_i \tilde w_j \,|x_i - x_j|^2
      = 2 \sum_i \tilde w_i \,|x_i - \bar x|^2 ,
\qquad r_i \equiv x_i / L ,
$$

where the second form, the variance identity, is what the code evaluates
in $O(N)$ (`rms_pairwise_distance` in `geometry.py`). The measure-weighted mean
$\bar x$ appears only inside this one scalar and is never used as a frame
origin. Because $L$ is a length of the geometry, a uniform rescale of the
points is invisible to everything downstream. A fixed constant does not do
that, and a statistic of the sampled points moves with the mesher.
@fig-isla-frame shows why a point statistic is a poor frame, and
@sec-isla-variants says why ISLA names no center at all.

ISLA states where a point is only *relative to other things*. The scaled
positions $r_i$ are used solely in differences $r_i - z_s$ against slice
anchors (idea 3). A common shift of every point therefore cancels exactly,
and translation invariance needs no centering. The only data a token starts
with, its **seed**, is the orientation of its normal against each global
direction, together with the global scalars,

$$
s_i \equiv \big[\,\hat n_i\!\cdot\!\hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat n_i\!\cdot\!\hat g_K,\ \sigma\,\big],
\qquad h_i^{(0)} = \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{embed}}(s_i):
$$

on the airfoil, "how much does this cell face the oncoming flow". With
$K = 0$ and $S = 0$ the seed is a constant and every distinction between
tokens comes from the relational invariants of idea 4.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-frame
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Why the frame must not be a point statistic. The two samplings of
#|   @fig-isla-quadrature, overlaid. The plain mean of the sampled positions
#|   (open gray markers) moves toward the leading edge when the sampling is
#|   clustered there, so a model whose coordinates are centered on it sees the
#|   whole body displaced. The measure-weighted centroid (blue) and the
#|   length unit $L$, the measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance (printed),
#|   are integrals and agree between the samplings to quadrature error. How
#|   to read this: ISLA uses no center at all, only the length unit; the
#|   centroid is drawn to show that an integral is stable where a point
#|   statistic is not. It does not show a trained model.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.6))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.2)
ax.plot(Ju["xy"][:, 0], Ju["xy"][:, 1], color=INK, lw=1.0)
cent = {}
for JJ, mk, lab in ((Ju, "o", "equal-arclength"), (Jm, "s", "clustered")):
    ax.plot(JJ["mid"][:, 0], JJ["mid"][:, 1], mk, ms=3.0, color=INK2 if mk == "o" else MUTED, alpha=0.8, label=f"{lab} sample points")
    cent[lab] = (JJ["mid"].mean(axis=0), (JJ["w"][:, None] * JJ["mid"]).sum(axis=0) / JJ["w"].sum())
    ax.plot(*cent[lab][0], mk, ms=11, mfc="white", mec=INK2, mew=2.0, zorder=5)
    ax.plot(*cent[lab][1], mk, ms=11, mfc=BLUE, mec=BLUE, mew=2.0, zorder=6)
pm_c = cent["clustered"][0]; pm_u = cent["equal-arclength"][0]; wc = cent["clustered"][1]
ax.annotate("plain mean of the clustered sample:\npulled toward the leading edge", xy=pm_c, xytext=(-1.6, -0.75), fontsize=8.5, color=INK2,
            ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.8))
ax.annotate("measure-weighted centroids of both samplings\n(the equal-arclength plain mean coincides with them)", xy=wc, xytext=(0.9, 0.75),
            fontsize=8.5, color=BLUE, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=BLUE, lw=0.8))
def rms_pairwise_distance(JJ):
    # the variance identity: sum_ij w_i w_j |x_i - x_j|^2 = 2 sum_i w_i |x_i - c|^2 with normalized weights
    wt = JJ["w"] / JJ["w"].sum(); c = (wt[:, None] * JJ["mid"]).sum(axis=0)
    return np.sqrt(2.0 * np.sum(wt * np.sum((JJ["mid"] - c) ** 2, axis=1)))
ax.text(-2.3, -1.02, f"length unit $L$ (RMS pairwise distance): {rms_pairwise_distance(Ju):.3f} (equal-arclength), {rms_pairwise_distance(Jm):.3f} (clustered)", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8.5)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Code correspondence"}
`gauge` is $L$, and `r` is $r_i$. `n_hat` and `g_hat` are the unit normal
and global directions. `log_w` is $\ell_i$. `invariants` is the seed $s_i$
(`_seed_invariants` in `physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/model.py`). The
magnitude $\lvert g_k \rvert$ is discarded: no fixed power of a global
vector's magnitude is a physical law (a pressure coefficient is degree zero
in the far-field speed, a dimensional pressure degree two), so a magnitude
that matters is passed as a global scalar and learned.
:::

## Idea 3: slices and their anchors {#sec-isla-slices}

**Attention over two hundred thousand tokens is too expensive and too
unstructured. Slice attention routes every token softly into a few hundred
slices, and each slice becomes one aggregate token.** In each layer, a
learned map of the normalized token state gives a routing logit
$\lambda_{is}$ for every token–slice pair (its form is the subject of
@sec-isla-routing-forms). A softmax *over tokens* for each slice, with the
measure bias of idea 1, gives the routing weights

$$
a_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda_{js} + \ell_j)} .
$$

Because the softmax runs over tokens, each slice's weights sum to one and
$\sum_i a_{is} f_i$ is a measure-weighted mean of the blue kind. ISLA adds
one thing Transolver does not have: from the same weights each slice forms
two vectors,

$$
z_s \equiv \sum_i a_{is}\, r_i, \qquad
m_s \equiv \frac{\sum_i a_{is}\, \hat n_i}{\lvert \sum_i a_{is}\, \hat n_i \rvert},
$$

its mean position and its mean normal direction: the slice's **anchor**.
Both are weighted sums of vectors that rotate with the body, with weights
that do not, so the anchors rotate with the body. They give each layer $M$
data-adaptive reference points ($M = 256$ by default in the class, 512 in the reference configuration). Idea 4 describes a
token's position by its relation to this constellation instead of by
coordinates. @sec-arch-routing-trained shows the learned routing of a
trained model on a car and on a solid specimen.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-slices
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Soft slices and their anchors, illustrated with six slices on the
#|   airfoil. Each cell is colored by the slice that gives it the most
#|   weight; the routing here is a hand-made function of position along the
#|   surface, standing in for the learned logits. Stars are the anchors, the
#|   measure-weighted mean position of each slice, with the slice's mean
#|   normal drawn as an arrow. How to read this: an anchor need not lie on the
#|   surface, and the assignment is soft (every cell has some weight in every
#|   slice); in the model there are 256 slices per layer and the logits are
#|   learned from the token states. The slice colors are labels only and
#|   carry none of the book's architecture hues.
#| code-fold: true
JJ = joukowski(n_cells=80)
s_arc = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(JJ["w"])]); s_mid = (s_arc[:-1] + s_arc[1:]) / 2; total = s_arc[-1]
n_sl = 6
centers = (np.arange(n_sl) + 0.5) / n_sl * total
d = np.abs(s_mid[:, None] - centers[None, :]); d = np.minimum(d, total - d)
logits = -(d / (0.06 * total)) ** 2
lw_ = np.log(JJ["w"])[:, None]
a = np.exp(logits + lw_); a /= a.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)          # softmax over points, per slice
z = (a[:, :, None] * JJ["mid"][:, None, :]).sum(axis=0)              # anchors
m = (a[:, :, None] * JJ["nrm"][:, None, :]).sum(axis=0); m /= np.linalg.norm(m, axis=1, keepdims=True)
six_slice_colors = plt.get_cmap("Dark2")(np.linspace(0, 1, 8))[[0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.8))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.4)
segs = np.stack([JJ["xy"][:-1], JJ["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[six_slice_colors[k] for k in a.argmax(axis=1)], linewidths=6, capstyle="butt", zorder=2))
for k in range(n_sl):
    ax.plot(*z[k], marker="*", ms=16, color=six_slice_colors[k], mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate("", xy=z[k] + 0.45 * m[k], xytext=z[k], arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=six_slice_colors[k], lw=1.8), zorder=4)
ax.text(0.0, -1.2, r"star: anchor position $z_s = \sum_i a_{is} r_i$;  arrow: anchor normal $m_s$", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why the softmax runs over points, and what read-back does differently"}
Routing normalizes over points so that a slice is an *average*, with the
measure bias making it a quadrature average. Reading back (idea 5)
normalizes over slices instead, with no measure bias, because there a point
is choosing *where to read*, not how much it weighs. Adding a constant to
every $\ell_i$ cancels in the routing ratio, and the same constant leaves
$L$ unchanged too, because the weights are normalized before they enter it.
So ISLA is invariant to a rescale of the weights alone as well as to a joint
geometric rescale (@sec-isla-contracts).
:::

### The two forms of the routing logit {#sec-isla-routing-forms}


**ISLA routes on a bounded cosine, which bounds each logit's scale and
removes the learning-rate ceiling of an unbounded logit, but does not by
itself prevent a routing collapse.** The routing logit is a learned function of the
normalized token state $\tilde h_i \equiv \mathrm{LN}(h_i)$: a fixed
temperature $T$ times the cosine between $\tilde h_i$ and a prototype $p_s$
per slice, so every logit lies in $[-T, T]$ whatever the weights do. The
prototypes are not fixed rows: each is a learned seed plus a centered,
bounded summary of the sample's own tokens, so the slices a block offers
adapt to the case in front of it while every logit keeps its bound
(@sec-arch-layer). An unbounded affine logit has no such bound:

$$
\lambda_{is} = T\,\frac{\tilde h_i \cdot p_s}{\lVert \tilde h_i \rVert\,\lVert p_s \rVert}
\quad (\text{the bounded cosine form},\ T = 10),
\qquad
\lambda_{is} = W_a \tilde h_i + b_a \quad (\text{the unbounded linear form}).
$$

Under the linear form the weights can grow without limit. As they grow,
each slice's softmax over points sharpens toward a single point, and each
point's preference sharpens toward a single slice. A sharper routing
concentrates the slice states, which sharpens the next block's routing.
Wider or deeper networks raise the gain of that loop. The linear form
therefore has a learning-rate *ceiling* that falls like one over the width
and at least as fast as one over the depth. Above the ceiling the
validation loss descends for some epochs and then rises to the **mean-field
plateau**, the loss of predicting each case's field mean. The checkpoint in
that state routes every point of every block to a single slice with all
anchors coincident. The relational invariants then carry no information,
and the network can emit only a per-case constant. The plateau is total
routing collapse, not a poorly conditioned optimum. Bounding the logits
removes the ceiling, which is what makes wide and deep ISLA trainable, but
the routing can still collapse when the token states it reads lose their
contrast. In lanes trained with the raw slice reads, on DeepJEB++ half of
the blocks route to one to five effective slices of 512 with coincident
anchors (@sec-surface-deepjeb), and on AeroZoo the routing's effective
support fell to 0.40 to 0.57 of its epoch-39 value by epoch 55 in blocks 5,
9 and 11 while the residual stream grew (@sec-using-lr,
@sec-nb-aerozoo-hlogit-verdict). The temperature is the class constant `ROUTING_TEMPERATURE`, 10. The frame and
head contracts do not depend on the routing form. The collapsed note below
is the one place in the book where the linear form appears with numbers.

::: {.callout-warning title="Trained with the raw slice reads"}
The trained checkpoints behind this chapter's numbers and pictures use the raw slice reads, in which the slice sublayer pools and broadcasts the raw token state rather than its LayerNorm, not the normalized reads of ISLA's reference configuration (@sec-isla-layer).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The learning-rate ceiling of the linear form, measured"}
```{python}
#| label: tbl-using-rate-ceiling
#| output: asis
import json
from pathlib import Path
C = json.load(open(Path("..") / "results" / "cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json"))["configurations"]
def cell(key):
    c = C[key]; m = c["pressure_l2_mean"]; seeds = c["pressure_l2_seeds"]
    if m is None: return "NaN / plateau"
    tag = "**" if m < 0.1 else ""
    return f"{tag}{m:.4f}{tag} ({', '.join(f'{s:.2f}' if s > 0.1 else f'{s:.4f}' for s in seeds)})"
rows = [
    ("384 wide, 12 layers", "5e-4", "1e-3", cell("isla|w384|d12|s256|lr1e-3"), "7.5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d12|s256|lr7.5e-4"), "5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d12|s256|lr5e-4")),
    ("768 wide, 12 layers", "2.5e-4", "5e-4", cell("isla|w768|d12|s256|lr5e-4"), "3.75e-4", cell("isla|w768|d12|s256|lr3.75e-4"), "2.5e-4", cell("isla|w768|d12|s256|lr2.5e-4")),
    ("384 wide, 24 layers", "2.5e-4", "5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d24|s256|lr5e-4"), "—", "—", "2.5e-4", cell("isla|w384|d24|s256|lr2.5e-4")),
    ("384 wide, 48 layers", "1.25e-4", "2.5e-4", "NaN / plateau", "—", "—", "1.25e-4", "NaN / plateau"),
]
out = "| configuration | width rule rate | above the rule | error | between | error | at the rule | error |\n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n"
for r in rows: out += "| " + " | ".join(r) + " |\n"
print(out)
print(": The learning-rate ceiling of the linear routing form, measured on the DrivAerML Surface task at 435 cars and 100,000 cells (the scaling budget), "
      "float32 at 500 epochs, surface-pressure error as the two-seed mean with the seeds in parentheses. A value near 0.75 is the mean-field plateau; bold values are clean "
      "training. The width rule rate is $10^{-3} \\times 192 / \\mathrm{width} \\times 12 / \\mathrm{layers}$ (@sec-using-lr). How to read this: each row is one width and depth, and the three rate columns bracket its ceiling; the 48-layer row has no "
      "float32 value because the lane above the rule went to NaN and the lane at the rule reached the plateau after a clean start. "
      "It says nothing about ISLA's cosine form, which trains every one of these configurations cleanly at the higher rate. "
      "Data: results/cap435_reduction_2026-09-20.json. {#tbl-using-rate-ceiling}")
```
:::

### What the trained routing looks like {#sec-arch-routing-trained}

**On a trained model a slice is a region of the body. A token's dominant
slice is a patch of surface with an anchor inside the body, the first
layer routes nearly everything into a handful of slices, and the deep
layers spread the mass over most of the 256 while each token stays soft.**
Every routing picture so far drew hand-made routing weights on the
airfoil. This section reads the real ones out of trained checkpoints, so
the reader can see what idea 3 promised. The instrument is a
wrapper around the routing softmax over tokens (`_softmax_over_points`), with
pre- and post-hooks on each `_SliceBlock` that delimit the two calls a block
makes, the provisional pass that places the anchors and the refined pass
(@sec-arch-layer). The block's second call is read. From the recorded refined logits,
the read-back weights $\pi_{is}$ (a softmax over the slices without the
measure bias) are each token's **soft assignment**. The
**dominant slice** of a token is $\arg\max_s \pi_{is}$. The **mass** of a
slice is $q_s \equiv \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \pi_{is}$, the slices' share of the
tokens, summing to one. The **effective number of slices** is
$M_{\mathrm{eff}} \equiv \exp(-\sum_s q_s \log q_s)$, which is 256 when
every slice carries the same mass and 1 when one slice carries all of it.
The anchors are the $z_s$ of idea 3, drawn in the dataset's coordinates. Each
checkpoint is the final one of a completed run of ISLA at 384 wide, 12
layers, 256 slices, cosine routing and learning rate 5e-4 (the
configuration the ladders hold, not the reference configuration of
@sec-using-config, whose routing has 512 slices), run in float32 on the
first case of its validation loader with the geometry kernel it trained
with. The numbers in this section are computed from the stored weights as
the page renders.

```{python}
#| label: setup-routing-trained
#| include: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
SL = RES / "probes" / "slices_2026-09-22"
PF = RES / "problem_figures_2026-09-22"
M_SL = 256

def load_slices(run):
    z = np.load(SL / f"{run}_case0.npz"); meta = json.load(open(SL / f"{run}_case0.json"))
    return {k: z[k] for k in z.files}, meta

def n_eff(q):
    return float(np.exp(-(q * np.log(q + 1e-30)).sum()))

SLICE_COLS = slice_colors(M_SL)

def partition_colors(dom, conf, floor=0.25):
    """Dominant-slice color, faded toward paper where the token is undecided (its largest pi_is is small)."""
    c = SLICE_COLS[dom].copy(); a = np.clip(conf / max(np.quantile(conf, 0.95), 1e-6), floor, 1.0)
    paper = np.array([0.96, 0.96, 0.95, 1.0])
    return a[:, None] * c + (1 - a[:, None]) * paper

def draw_anchors(ax, d, li, scale=1.0, dims=(0, 1), s=50):
    q = d["q"][li]; active = np.flatnonzero(q > 1.0 / M_SL); A = d["anchors"][li][active] * scale
    ax.scatter(A[:, dims[0]], A[:, dims[1]], marker="*", s=s, c=SLICE_COLS[active], edgecolors=INK, linewidths=0.45, zorder=5)
    return len(active)

DR, DRm = load_slices("ref_isla_r1_dr435_seed42")
T2, T2m = load_slices("so_t2d_isla_r1_frame_n64_seed42")
AF, AFm = load_slices("ref_isla_r1_af_seed42")
LG, LGm = load_slices("so_lug_isla_r1_n300_seed43")
L_REF_DR = json.load(open(PF / "drivaer.json"))["L_ref"]        # the recipe divides DrivAerML positions by L_ref = 5 m
RUNS = {"DrivAerML Surface task, 435 cars": (DR, DRm), "AirfRANS interior task, 800 airfoils": (AF, AFm),
        "PLAID Tensile2d, 64 cases (the pose-prior diagnostic model, @sec-pose-prior)": (T2, T2m), "GINOT lug, 300 cases": (LG, LGm)}
```

#| label: fig-routing-partition-drivaer

#|   subset drawn), each colored by its dominant slice at the first, sixth and
#|   last slice layer; a token whose largest soft assignment is small is faded
#|   toward the paper. Stars are the anchors $z_s$ of the slices whose mass
#|   exceeds the uniform share $1/M$, in the slice's color. How to read this:
#|   slice colors are labels and repeat (twenty hues for 256 slices), so two
#|   distant patches of one hue are usually different slices; what the picture
#|   shows is the granularity and placement of the partition, not the identity

P = DR["points"][DR["keep"]] * L_REF_DR
layers = [int(i) for i in DR["top_layers"]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 7.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.25))
for ax, li in zip(axes, layers):
    depth_scatter(ax, P[:, [0, 2]], P[:, 1], partition_colors(DR["dominant"][li].astype(int), DR["pi_max"][li].astype(float)), s=2.0)
    map_axes(ax)
    n_act = draw_anchors(ax, DR, li, scale=L_REF_DR, dims=(0, 2))
    ax.set_title(f"layer {li + 1} of 12: effective number of slices {n_eff(DR['q'][li]):.0f}; {n_act} slices above the uniform mass (stars: their anchors)", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set_ylabel("z [m]")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("x [m]  (far-field flow along $+x$)")
plt.show()

```{python}
#| label: fig-routing-weights-drivaer
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Three individual slices of the sixth layer on the same car: the soft
#|   assignment $\pi_{is}$ of every token to the slice, as heat, for the three
#|   slices that are the dominant slice of the most tokens, each seen from the
#|   side (left) and from below (right). The star is the slice's anchor. How to
#|   read this: a slice is a soft region, brightest at its core and fading
#|   over its neighbors; the anchor is the routing-weighted mean position of
#|   the region and sits inside the body when the region wraps around it. The
#|   largest territories of this layer are on the wheels and the underbody,
#|   where the surface mesh is finest and the sampled tokens densest, which is
#|   why the view from below is drawn. Each panel's color scale runs to the
#|   slice's own 99.9th percentile of $\pi_{is}$; the printed $q_s$ is the
#|   slice's mass, its share of all tokens. Data:
#|   results/probes/slices_2026-09-22/ref_isla_r1_dr435_seed42_case0.npz.
#| code-fold: true
li_pos = 1; L6 = int(DR["top_layers"][li_pos]); ts = DR["top_slices"][li_pos][:3]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(8, 5.8), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.6, wspace=0.08, width_ratios=[1, 1]))
for j, (ax_side, ax_below) in enumerate(axes):
    pi = DR["top_pi"][li_pos][:, j].astype(float); vmax = max(0.2, float(np.quantile(pi, 0.999)))
    sc = depth_scatter(ax_side, P[:, [0, 2]], P[:, 1], pi, s=1.6, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=vmax)
    depth_scatter(ax_below, P[:, [0, 1]], -P[:, 2], pi, s=1.6, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=vmax)
    a = DR["anchors"][L6][ts[j]] * L_REF_DR
    ax_side.plot(a[0], a[2], marker="*", ms=12, color=WHITE, mec=INK, mew=0.8, zorder=5)
    ax_below.plot(a[0], a[1], marker="*", ms=12, color=WHITE, mec=INK, mew=0.8, zorder=5)
    for ax in (ax_side, ax_below):
        map_axes(ax)
    n_dom = int((DR["dominant"][L6] == ts[j]).sum())
    ax_side.set_title(f"slice {int(ts[j])}: $q_s$ = {DR['q'][L6][ts[j]]:.3f}, dominant for {n_dom:,} of {len(P):,} tokens; side view", fontsize=8.2)
    ax_below.set_title("the same slice from below", fontsize=8.2, loc="right")
    ax_side.set_ylabel("z [m]"); ax_below.set_ylabel("y [m]"); ax_below.yaxis.set_label_position("right"); ax_below.yaxis.tick_right()
    cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=[ax_side, ax_below], fraction=0.015, pad=0.08); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
    cb.set_label(r"$\pi_{is}$ [–]", fontsize=8)
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("x [m]")
plt.show()

    f"(each normal against the far-field direction), refined by the geometry against anchors formed from that same seed, and a car's "
    f"surface offers few distinct values of it. From the "
    f"second layer on, the token states carry position through the relational invariants, and the effective number rises to "
    f"{min(ne_dr[1:6]):.0f} to {max(ne_dr[1:6]):.0f} in layers 2 to 6 and {min(ne_dr[6:]):.0f} to {max(ne_dr[6:]):.0f} in layers 7 to 12. "
    f"The specimen model, whose seed already carries the boundary labels, two given directions and six global scalars, starts at {ne_t2[0]:.0f} "
    f"and stays between {min(ne_t2):.0f} and {max(ne_t2):.0f}. The assignment is soft throughout: in the sixth layer "
    f"{undecided(DR, 5):.0f}% of the car's tokens and {undecided(T2, 5):.0f}% of the specimen's give no single slice more than half "
    f"their weight, and in the last layer {undecided(DR, 11):.0f}% and {undecided(T2, 11):.0f}%. Anchors sit inside the body, not on "
    f"it, as the weighted mean of a patch that wraps a wheel or a neck must. These are descriptions of one validation case of one "
    f"seed per model; they show the granularity of the learned partition and are not a claim about accuracy."
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How the weights were read"}
The wrapper records the input and output of every call of
`_softmax_over_points`. A slice block calls it twice: once with the
provisional logits (used only to place the anchors) and once with
the refined logits. Forward pre-hooks on the blocks record where
each block's calls start and end, and the block's last call is read. Its
input is $\lambda'_{is} + \ell_i$. Subtracting the measure bias $\ell_i$
(taken from the block's second argument) and normalizing over slices gives
$\pi_{is}$ exactly as the refinement computes it. The numbers here are per
block.
The recorded arrays are stored
subsampled to 60,000 tokens per case for the pictures. The masses and
effective numbers are computed over every token before subsampling. Probe:
`results/probes/slices_2026-09-22/slices_probe.py`.
:::

## Idea 4: relational invariants {#sec-isla-relational}

**Everything a token learns about its position, it learns from a handful of
scalars per anchor.** For each token–anchor pair, with
$\rho_{is} \equiv r_i - z_s$ the separation and $\hat\rho_{is}$ its
direction, the layer forms

$$
\xi_{is} \equiv \big[\,
\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\ \log\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_K,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat n_i,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\! m_s,\ \hat n_i\!\cdot\! m_s
\,\big],
$$

which is $5 + K$ numbers, six with one global direction. They say how far
the anchor is, on two scales, whether it lies along or against the global
direction, whether it lies in front of the token's face or behind it,
whether the token lies in front of the anchor's face, and whether the two
faces agree. Each is a norm or a dot product of vectors that rotate
together, so each is unchanged by any rotation or translation of the body.
Each is built from a difference of positions, so no frame origin appears.
@fig-isla-relational draws them for one token and one anchor.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-relational
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The relational invariants of one token against one anchor. The token
#|   (black dot) has normal $n_i$; the anchor (star) has position $z_s$ and
#|   normal $m_s$; the separation $\rho_{is}$ runs from anchor to token. The
#|   six scalars ISLA forms are the length of $\rho$ (and its logarithm) and
#|   four cosines: of $\rho$ against the global direction $\hat g_1$, against
#|   $n_i$, against $m_s$, and of $n_i$ against $m_s$. How to read this: every
#|   one of these numbers is the same after any rotation or translation of the
#|   page; no coordinate axis appears in any of them.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.5)
ax.plot(JJ["xy"][:, 0], JJ["xy"][:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.2)
i = 22; k = 4                      # a token on the upper surface, the anchor mid-chord on the lower surface
xi, ni = JJ["mid"][i], JJ["nrm"][i]; zs, ms = z[k], m[k]
rho = xi - zs; rho_hat = rho / np.linalg.norm(rho); g = JJ["g_hat"]
ax.plot(*xi, "o", ms=8, color=INK, zorder=6)
ax.plot(*zs, marker="*", ms=18, color=VIOLET, mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=6)
arrow = lambda p, v, c, lw=1.8: ax.annotate("", xy=p + v, xytext=p, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=c, lw=lw), zorder=5)
arrow(zs, rho, INK2, 1.6); arrow(xi, 0.5 * ni, INK); arrow(zs, 0.5 * ms, VIOLET)
arrow(np.array([-2.3, 1.05]), 0.6 * g, INK, 2.0)
ax.text(-2.3, 1.25, r"$\hat g_1$ (global direction)", fontsize=10, color=INK)
ax.text(*(xi + 0.6 * ni + [0.0, -0.08]), r"$n_i$", fontsize=11, color=INK, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(*(zs + 0.6 * ms + [0.0, -0.08]), r"$m_s$", fontsize=11, color=VIOLET, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(*(zs + 0.5 * rho + [0.15, 0.0]), r"$\rho_{is} = r_i - z_s$", fontsize=11, color=INK2, ha="left", va="center", path_effects=halo())
ax.text(*(xi + [-0.12, 0.0]), "token $i$", fontsize=10, color=INK, ha="right", va="center")
ax.text(*(zs + [0.12, 0.0]), "anchor $s$", fontsize=10, color=VIOLET, ha="left", va="center")
vals = [(r"$|\rho_{is}|$", f"{np.linalg.norm(rho):.2f}"), (r"$\log|\rho_{is}|$", f"{np.log(np.linalg.norm(rho)):+.2f}"),
        (r"$\hat\rho_{is}\cdot\hat g_1$", f"{rho_hat @ g:+.2f}"), (r"$\hat\rho_{is}\cdot n_i$", f"{rho_hat @ ni:+.2f}"),
        (r"$\hat\rho_{is}\cdot m_s$", f"{rho_hat @ ms:+.2f}"), (r"$n_i\cdot m_s$", f"{ni @ ms:+.2f}")]
ax.text(1.35, 1.4, r"$\xi_{is}$, the six relational invariants", fontsize=9.5, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
for j, (lab, v) in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(1.4, 1.15 - 0.27 * j, lab, fontsize=10, color=INK, va="center"); ax.text(2.45, 1.15 - 0.27 * j, v, fontsize=10, color=INK2, ha="right", va="center")
plt.show()
```

The invariants do two jobs in a layer. A linear map of $\xi_{is}$ to one
scalar, with a learned weight vector $w_g$ and bias $b_g$, **refines the
routing**, $\lambda'_{is} = \lambda_{is} + w_g \cdot \xi_{is} + b_g$, so
that a slice can prefer tokens that are near its anchor, or along the global
direction from it, or facing it. The routing weights $a'_{is}$ are
recomputed with the same measure-weighted softmax. And the invariants are
**pooled back** to the token (idea 5), so it learns where it sits relative
to the slices it belongs to.

## Idea 5: the slice layer, assembled {#sec-isla-layer}

**A slice layer sends information up from tokens to slices, transforms it
there, and sends it back down together with the geometry.** With the
refined routing weights, the slice state is the measure-weighted mean of the
normalized token states $\tilde h_i \equiv \mathrm{LN}(h_i)$, the same
normalized state the routing reads, passed through a per-slice MLP:

$$
Z_s = \sum_i a'_{is}\, \tilde h_i, \qquad Z_s \leftarrow Z_s + \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{slice}}(\mathrm{LN}(Z_s)).
$$

Reading back uses a softmax *over slices* for each token, without the
measure bias, and pools both the slice states and the relational
invariants:

$$
\pi_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda'_{is})}{\sum_t \exp(\lambda'_{it})}, \qquad
b_i = \sum_s \pi_{is}\, Z_s, \qquad
\gamma_i = W_f \Big(\sum_s \pi_{is}\, \xi_{is}\Big) + b_f,
$$

$$
h_i \leftarrow h_i + W_b\,[\,\tilde h_i;\ b_i;\ \gamma_i\,], \qquad
h_i \leftarrow h_i + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(h_i)).
$$

The token ends the layer knowing which slices it belongs to, what those
slices contain, and where it sits relative to their anchors. A stack of such
layers, pre-LayerNorm with residual connections, is the encoder. Both
sublayers are pre-LayerNorm in the full sense: the slice sublayer routes,
pools and broadcasts from $\tilde h_i$ alone, so the raw state $h_i$
enters a layer only through the residual identity and the token MLP's
LayerNorm. The update each sublayer adds is then a function of the
normalized state and the geometry, unchanged when a token's state is
rescaled. ISLA runs one routing per layer.

The pooled invariants are projected *after* pooling. This is exact because
the projection is affine and $\pi_{is}$ sums to one. The identity and the
memory it saves are in @sec-arch-layer.

## Idea 6: fields of any rank from an equivariant basis {#sec-isla-heads}

**The network's state is made of invariants, so an output of tensor rank
$r$ must be assembled from tensor products of $r$ vectors that rotate
with the body, with invariant coefficients.** A single linear head on the
normalized final state produces every output's coefficients. An output
declared with rank $r$ is the contraction of its coefficients with products
of $r$ vectors from the token's basis,

$$
c_i = W_h\, \mathrm{LN}(h_i), \qquad
T_i = \sum_{j_1 \dots j_r} c_{i\,j_1 \dots j_r}\,
t_{i j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes t_{i j_r} \;+\; \text{isotropic terms}, \qquad
\{t_{ij}\} = \big\{\hat g_1, \dots, \hat g_K,\ \hat n_i,\ \hat u_i,\
e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat n_i),\ e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat g_k)\big\}.
$$

Rank 0 is the coefficient itself (pressure). Rank 1 is a vector over the
$m = 2K + 3$ basis vectors (wall shear stress, five coefficients with one
global direction). Rank 2 is a matrix over their $m^2$ outer products plus
the identity. For a symmetric spec it is a matrix over the $m(m+1)/2$
symmetrized products plus the identity (a stress tensor, sixteen
coefficients with one global direction). Ranks 3 and 4 follow the same
rule, with the three products of Kronecker deltas as the isotropic terms of
rank 4 (their symmetric sum for a symmetric spec). Three of the basis
vectors are directions the token already has: the global direction(s), its
own normal, and $\hat u_i$. The last is the **radial** direction from the
token's own soft anchor to the token. A separate routing softmax assigns
the token to slices, and $u_i = r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is} z_s$ is a
difference of positions, so no center appears. These already span space
generically. The complements $e_\theta(\hat u, \hat a)$, the part of
$-\hat a$ orthogonal to $\hat u$, keep the expansion well conditioned where
the three are nearly coplanar. They are left unnormalized, so they vanish
smoothly where $\hat u \parallel \hat a$ and no direction field on the
sphere has to be combed. Every basis vector is a *true* vector (no cross
product among them), so every product is a true tensor and the output
transforms as $R^{\otimes r}$ under rotations *and* reflections. The head
is O(3)-covariant, not only SO(3)-covariant.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-basis
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The vector head's basis at one token, in the plane of the airfoil. The
#|   token's wall shear stress is a linear combination, with learned
#|   invariant coefficients, of directions the token already owns: the
#|   global direction $\hat g_1$, its normal $n_i$, and the radial direction
#|   $\hat u_i$ from its soft anchor (star), together with the complements
#|   $e_\theta, e_\phi$ (the in-plane complement is drawn). How to read this:
#|   rotate the page and every basis vector rotates with it while the
#|   coefficients, being invariants, do not; that is the whole of the
#|   covariance proof. It does not show a trained head.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.8))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.5)
ax.plot(JJ["xy"][:, 0], JJ["xy"][:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.2)
i = 18; xi, ni = JJ["mid"][i], JJ["nrm"][i]
beta = np.exp(-((s_mid[i] - centers) / (0.35 * total)) ** 2); beta /= beta.sum()   # a soft assignment spread over slices
anchor = (beta[:, None] * z).sum(axis=0); u = xi - anchor; u_hat = u / np.linalg.norm(u)
e_th = -(ni - (ni @ u_hat) * u_hat); e_th_hat = e_th / np.linalg.norm(e_th)
ax.plot(*anchor, marker="*", ms=16, color=VIOLET, mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=6)
ax.plot(*xi, "o", ms=8, color=INK, zorder=6)
arrow(anchor, u, INK2, 1.2)
for v, c, lab in ((g, INK, r"$\hat g_1$"), (ni, BLUE, r"$\hat n_i$"), (u_hat, VIOLET, r"$\hat u_i$"), (e_th_hat, AQUA, r"$e_\theta(\hat u_i,\hat n_i)$")):
    arrow(xi, 0.6 * v, c, 2.0); ax.text(*(xi + 0.75 * v), lab, fontsize=11, color=c, ha="center", va="center", path_effects=halo())
ax.text(*(anchor + [0.0, -0.2]), "token's soft anchor", fontsize=9, color=VIOLET, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(*(anchor + 0.5 * u + [0.08, -0.05]), r"$u_i = r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is} z_s$", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2, va="top", path_effects=halo())
ax.text(0.2, -1.15, r"$v_i = \sum_j c_{ij} B_{ij}$: learned invariant coefficients $c_{ij}$ times body-fixed directions $B_{ij}$", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reflections and pseudotensors"}
Every backbone invariant is a norm or a dot product of true vectors, so
every *scalar* output is invariant under reflections as well as rotations,
and every even-parity output is a true tensor. A quantity that flips sign
under a mirror (a vorticity, a magnetic field, a torque) is a pseudotensor
and is declared with `parity: odd`: its basis is the set of products with
exactly one *pseudovector* factor, the cross products $\hat g_k \times \hat
n_i$, $\hat g_k \times \hat u_i$, $\hat n_i \times \hat u_i$ of the
primary true vectors ($\binom{K+2}{2}$ of them, three with one global
direction), plus the Levi-Civita symbol at rank 3. Such an output
transforms as $\det(R)\, R^{\otimes r}$, which is the pseudotensor law. A
head that mixed both kinds of basis vector in one output would be
covariant under proper rotations only. The parity is a declaration, so a
true vector never pays for a pseudovector's basis.
:::

**The contract has a clause for outputs that are components: a component
is only ever a view of a tensor.** A scalar head can represent only
invariants of the input vector set, so a stress component $\sigma_{ij} =
e_i^{\mathsf T} \sigma\, e_j$, which is an invariant of that set only once
it is augmented with the frame vectors $e_i, e_j$, is representable only
when the frame is an input or when the head produces the tensor $\sigma$
itself and the components are read off afterwards. ISLA takes the second
route: the target is declared with its rank
(`stress: {rank: 2, symmetric: true}`), the head expands it in the
symmetrized outer products of the true basis vectors together with the
identity, and no laboratory frame enters anywhere. The clause binds on
solids whose targets are stress components and is measured there
(@sec-interior-tensile2d).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The tensor head, and the route that is rejected"}
With $m = 2K + 3$ true basis vectors the symmetric rank-2 output is

$$
\sigma_i = \sum_{j \le k} c_{ijk}\, \tfrac{1}{2}\big(t_{ij} t_{ik}^{\mathsf T} + t_{ik} t_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\big) + c_{i0}\, I,
$$

with $m(m+1)/2 + 1$ invariant coefficients from the same linear head
(seven with no global direction, sixteen with one). The recipe reads the
laboratory components the dataset stores off the predicted tensor
(`symmetric_tensor` targets with a `components` mapping). The tests hold
the covariance to $10^{-12}$ in float64 for random rotations and mirrors,
for every rank and parity the class admits.

The other conceivable route, passing the dataset's own axes as global
directions so that scalar heads can produce the components, also keeps the
covariance contract intact, but it is rejected: those axes are not a datum
of the PDE, and a model that needs them has been told the pose of the
training set (@sec-pose-inputs). Pressure, von Mises stress and plastic
strain are invariants and need none of this. GeoTransolver reads absolute
coordinates and has no such clause, which is why the aerodynamic datasets,
whose outputs are a true scalar and a vector, never expose it.
:::

### Inputs of any rank enter through invariants {#sec-isla-inputs-rank}

**The same rule runs backwards at the input: a boundary field of rank 1
or 2 reaches the network only through its invariants against the
directions the token already has.** A per-cell vector $v_i$ (a prescribed
traction, an applied load) contributes to the token's seed its cosines with
the token's frame, $v_i \cdot \hat n_i$ and $v_i \cdot \hat g_k$, its norm
$\lvert v_i \rvert$, and its dot products with the token's other vector
inputs. Inside every slice layer, where the token-to-anchor direction
$\hat\rho_{is}$ exists, it contributes $v_i \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$ beside the
$\hat n_i \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$ and $\hat g_k \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$ of
@sec-isla-relational. An input vector is treated exactly as the normal is,
by one helper that contracts every per-token vector with the anchor
direction. A per-cell rank-2 field $T_i$ (a prescribed stress) contributes
to the seed the bilinear contractions $a^{\mathsf T} T_i b$ over the frame
vectors $a, b \in \{\hat n_i, \hat g_k\}$, $\operatorname{tr} T_i$ and
$\lVert T_i \rVert_F$. In the layers it contributes
$\hat\rho^{\mathsf T} T_i \hat\rho$, $\hat\rho \cdot T_i \hat n_i$ and
$\hat\rho \cdot T_i \hat g_k$. The last two are the derived true vectors
$T_i \hat n_i$ and $T_i \hat g_k$ contracted with the anchor direction, so
they ride on the same helper. Only true vectors appear on the input side,
no cross products, so every input invariant is unchanged by a reflection,
and pseudotensor inputs are refused. A rank-0 input is the scalar itself.
The per-query fields of the interior modes enter the same way through their
own embedding. The global inputs are the special case where a rank-1 field
is a direction shared by every token (it is normalized and joins the head
basis) and a rank-0 field is a parameter appended to every seed. The cost
is one scalar per slice per extra vector in the geometry region. That is
why the fused kernel takes the global directions and the rank-1 per-token
inputs as one set of at most four vectors per token, and hands a model
with rank-2 per-token inputs, or more vectors than that, to the eager
region (@sec-arch-switches). A dataset that stores a boundary vector
component by component (a prescribed displacement or traction per axis)
stacks the components into one rank-1 field in the dataset pipeline
(`StackScalarFields`). Feeding laboratory components as scalars leaks the
frame.

## Why ISLA has no center {#sec-isla-variants}

**ISLA states position only relative to its own anchors because a PDE does
not know what "the body" is.** The area-weighted centroid of a surface is
not a point the physics distinguishes. For an open or truncated boundary, a
multi-body scene, or a boundary with structure at every scale, that
centroid is an artifact of where the domain was cut, and a frame built on
it carries the artifact into every invariant. The relative frame presumes
none of this. Positions enter only as differences $r_i - z_s$ against
anchors that are themselves measure-weighted means, so no origin is ever
named. The one place a mean position appears, inside the length unit $L$,
is a scalar. A center taken from a sample statistic rather than an integral
is worse than useless under a change of sampling (@fig-isla-frame). A
center taken from an integral is harmless on a closed single body and
meaningless everywhere else. The class therefore has no centered frame. The
two invariances this construction buys, pose and discretization, are the
subject of @sec-invariances.

## The forward pass on one page {#sec-isla-forward}

**Every symbol of the six ideas has one identifier in the code, and
@sec-architecture is the dictionary.** That chapter states the pass stage
by stage with the shape of every tensor (@fig-isla-pass), opens up the slice
layer step by step (@fig-isla-layer), counts where the parameters are
(@tbl-isla-params) and lists the switches (@sec-arch-switches). The six
ideas here map onto its stages as follows. Idea 1 is the measure bias of
every routing softmax (stages 3b, 3f, 4). Idea 2 is stage 1. Ideas 3 to 5
are stage 3. Idea 6 is stages 4 and 5.

## The contracts, as tests {#sec-isla-contracts}

**Each contract is a property of the code, verified in double precision on
random weights and a random anisotropic point cloud, not a property of a
trained checkpoint.** The tests live in
`test/experimental/models/isla/test_isla.py`, `test_isla_global_inputs.py`,
`test_isla_heads.py` (every output rank and parity) and
`test_isla_inputs.py` (rank-1 and rank-2 inputs, geometry and fields
transformed together). The fixture is a 3-layer, 32-slice, width-64 model
in float64 on 500 points with random normals, global direction and
weights.

| contract | test | tolerance |
|---|---|---|
| rotation covariance: scalars unchanged, vectors $v \mapsto vQ^\top$ for a proper rotation $Q$ | `test_rotation_equivariance`, `test_frame_contracts` | $10^{-10}$ |
| translation invariance, with no centering anywhere | `test_translation_invariance`, `test_translation_invariance_alone` | $10^{-10}$ / $10^{-11}$ |
| geometric-scale invariance: points $\times k$ (with or without areas $\times k^2$) leave every output unchanged; so does a rescale of the areas alone, because the unit is normalized | `test_rms_distance_scale_contracts`, `test_measure_scale_invariance`, `test_geometric_scale_equivariance` | $10^{-10}$ / $10^{-9}$ |
| the length unit stays finite under refinement of a boundary whose total measure diverges (Koch curve) | `test_rms_distance_converges_on_koch_curve_where_total_measure_diverges` | converges |
| re-representing the boundary measure on finer cells leaves the interior prediction unchanged | `test_query_mass_refinement_invariance` | $10^{-10}$, rtol 0 |
| prediction points off the surface keep every contract | `test_interior_contracts`, `test_interior_task_contracts` | $10^{-11}$ / $10^{-6}$ |
| several boundary meshes are one token set; a mesh without stored measures uses its geometric quadrature | `test_several_boundary_meshes_are_one_token_set`, `test_no_effective_measures_is_the_geometric_quadrature` | $10^{-10}$ |
| zero and several global vectors; global scalars; magnitude invariance | `test_isla_global_inputs.py` | $10^{-10}$ |
| pool-then-project equals project-then-pool | `test_geo_pool_then_project_is_exact` | $10^{-12}$ |
| every parameter receives a gradient; heads run under bf16 autocast | `test_all_parameters_receive_gradients`, `test_head_runs_under_bf16_autocast` | exact / finite |
| the same contracts in two dimensions, reflection included | `test_two_dimensional_contracts_rotation_translation_magnitude_and_reflection` | $10^{-4}$ |

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="What is not a contract"}
- **Reflection covariance of vectors** (see idea 6).
- **The magnitude of a global vector input**: discarded by design.
- **Query independence in the interacting configuration.** Every surface
  point is an interacting token, and so is every interior query in the
  reported configuration, so the prediction at a point depends on which
  other points are in the request, and that configuration is deployed at
  its training query count (@sec-interior-companion). The read-only
  interior model, ISLA-DTT, has query independence as a contract by
  construction: its prediction points read the slices and never write
  into them (@sec-arch-passive-decoder,
  `test_query_independent_interior_contracts`).
- **Completeness of the representation.** The anchors are first moments,
  so two non-congruent arrangements with the same first moments are
  indistinguishable to every layer
  (`results/isla_first_moment_collision_2026-09-08.json`). The collision is
  not established as the cause of any measured deficit.
- **Finite-precision residual on the deployed path.** The tests run in
  float64. On the trained GPU path in float32 the contracts hold to 3e-5 at
  worst over 24 validation cars (two checkpoints, random rigid motions).
  Under the bf16 autocast the recipe trains with, the residual is material:
  4% of the pressure prediction and 7% of the wall-shear vector on average,
  against a 2.3% rounding difference between bf16 and float32 with no
  motion at all, so most of it is ordinary bf16 rounding. "Exact" describes
  the algebra and the float32 path. Where a contract is load-bearing, infer
  in float32 (@sec-using-sampler; results/precres_2026-09-18.json).
:::
